        **Abstract**: Decentralization is understood both by professionals in the blockchain industry and general users as a core design goal
of permissionless ledgers. However, its meaning is far from universally agreed, and often it is easier to get opinions on
what it is not, rather than what it is. In this paper, we solicit deﬁnitions of ‘decentralization’ and ‘decentralization theatre’
from blockchain node operators. Key to a deﬁnition is asking about effective decentralization strategies, as well as
those that are ineffective, sometimes deliberately so. Malicious, deceptive or at the least incompetent strategies are
commonly referred to by the term ‘decentralization theatre.’ Finally, we ask what is being decentralized. We ﬁnd that
most operators conceive decentralization as existing broadly on a technical and a governance axis. Isolating relevant
variables, we collapse the categories to network topology and governance topology, or the structure of decision-making
power. Our key ﬁnding is that ‘decentralization’ alone does not affect ledger immutability or systemic robustness.
Keywords:
blockchain, decentralization, DAO, governance, security, voting systems, economic ﬁnality
Supplementary material: Node operators survey and interviews - see appendix
Acknowledgments: Thanks to all operators that responded to the survey; JP Vergne for lively discussions
on decentralization; the Game of Nodes; schultzie, null and usurper.
1 INTRODUCTION
In this paper, we deﬁne ‘decentralization’, and analyse whether or not it has any impact on the rewrite resis-
tance of permissionless ledgers. We advance deﬁnitions for ‘decentralization’ based on our own analysis,
and compare these with deﬁnitions sourced from ﬁeldwork. This ﬁeldwork took the form of semi-structured
audio interviews, and an anonymous online survey. Blockchains, whether consensus is achieved by Proof-
of-Work, (delegated) Proof-of-Stake, or another security mechanism, require nodes to operate, and conse-
quently, we have focussed on the technical practitioners that operate these nodes for our ﬁeldwork, rather
than a more general survey of stakeholders.
Decentralization, while difﬁcult to deﬁne, is a core tenet of blockchain technology, and is deﬁned via
protocol-enforced incentives and technical means as well as by non-technical measures.
We propose
potential ways of understanding decentralization in §2.2, and document the views of node operators on what
it means in the real world in §3. Throughout, we address the views of node operators on decentralization,
the responsibilities of validators, and their role within the organisational dynamics of a network.
Finally, to make the implicit explicit, we offer a model for roles in the typical structure of a Proof-of-Stake
blockchain (§4.1.1). We use our interviews to inform not only the identiﬁcation of personas, but also support
analysis of the reported dynamics between them. Though we focus on the Cosmos Ecosystem, due to our
recruitment methodology, much of our analysis can be applied to any network that uses Proof-of-Stake, or
speciﬁcally, Delegated Proof-of-Stake as its security mechanism.
We theorize that, contrary to a general assumption by node operators that increased decentralization re-
sults in increased rewrite resistance, different network and governance topologies simply result in different
manifestations of ledger rewrites (§4.1.3 and §4.3). For example, consortium ledgers might feature the risk
that an authority uses its position to force change, and permissionless ledgers might be at risk of takeover by
foundations, developer groups, or stakeholder blocs. Crucially, our breakdown of the two axes of decentral-
ization, network topology and governance topology (§4.2), that can be analysed both ex-ante and ex-post
relies on a simple heuristic, asking the question ‘decentralization of what?’

2 METHODOLOGY AND CONTEXT
2.1 Methodology
We undertook a survey of node operators from organisations that run validator nodes. An anonymous survey
was posted to private validator communication channels, private threads and private forums for networks in
the Cosmos Ecosystem. Typically, these threads are kept up-to-date by core teams and foundations, and
are invite-only. The reason is that these channels are often used for coordination in the event of a security
patch, cyber attack or other critical event. However, this also meant that targeting these channels, even for
an anonymous survey, resulted in a large pool of organisations and their users.
It is hard to establish the total pool of unique operators in a given set of channels, since many operate
on several chains, but we estimate the reach of our recruitment to have been in the hundreds. For context,
using node data we collected on the 3rd of May 2024, across 62 Cosmos chains tracked by the chain explorer
Mintscan, there were 2,275 unique validators1.
Additionally, we recruited respondents from the same channels, but this time both inside and outside of
Cosmos, to take part in a semi-structured interview. Despite recruiting more widely than the survey, the goal
was still to target operators that were familiar with the Cosmos stack and Tendermint, its consensus protocol.
In these interviews, a series of questions and discussion areas were introduced, with the interviewer prompt-
ing for clariﬁcations where needed. After transcription, the source audio was deleted and a UUID assigned
to the transcription.
However, in spite of the measures taken to safeguard respondents, the number of responses was mod-
est, with 35 surveys ﬁlled out, including 14 partial responses. Comparatively, recruitment for semi-structured
interviews was better, as there was initial concern that no volunteers would come forward. In the end, we had
six interviewees.
The low number of responses is likely because the blockchain space retains a generally careful approach
to operational security and privacy, and also because public statements on governance and ‘decentralization’
can be politically charged. At worst, for a respondent there is the risk not only that their identity is revealed, but
also of harassment or threats. For this reason, collecting the data while protecting the identity of respondents
was of paramount concern. As it was, relatively few operators were comfortable to respond out of a pool of
hundreds, resulting in a small dataset.
The questions used for both survey and semi-structured interviews can be found in the Appendix.
2.2 Decentralization
The most important context for this discussion is to deﬁne ‘decentralization’, and provide some background
to frame how our respondents approached the loaded term.
The meaning of ‘decentralization’ is far from universally agreed. The ISO deﬁnition of a decentralized
system (3.20)[17] is a good starting point, a “distributed system (3.24) wherein control is distributed among
the persons or organizations participating in the operation of the system.” This does immediately beg the
question however of how that control is distributed. The ISO deﬁnition simply notes, “the distribution of control
among persons or organizations participating in the system is determined by the system’s design.”
Gochhayat et al.,[14] conceive of a blockchain system as consisting of a governance layer, a network layer,
and a storage layer, and analyse the degree of decentrality at each:
Decentralized systems are a subset of distributed systems where multiple authorities control different
components and no authority is fully trusted by all. Decentrality is a property related to the control over
the system. Better decentralization means higher resistance against censorship and tampering.
Of the three layers they enumerate, their deﬁnition of governance layer is the single most important for our
analysis, relating more strictly to voting power in the protocol, in their case Proof-of-Work, by “nodes partici-
pating in the block creation or mining process” and their hash rate. This is similar to other deﬁnitions such as
Lin et al.,[21] which also focus on distribution of mining power. Gochhayat et al.[14] also advance deﬁnitions
of network and storage layers that are useful for our analysis. The network layer involves control of network
topology, bandwidth and block dissemination, factors more important in probabilistic ﬁnality, and less impor-
tant in a Delegated Proof-of-Stake network with absolute ﬁnality. The storage layer meanwhile relates to node
location, datacentre or cloud provider, which incidentally maps closely on to many deﬁnitions of decentraliza-
tion given in our ﬁeldwork by node operators, who often mentioned hardware and geographic dispersion of
nodes.

A better deﬁnition then might be a multi-faceted one, that takes in both technical and economic factors,
such as that advanced by JP Vergne. Vergne attacks the deﬁnition from a different angle, identifying theatrical
modes for the discussion of decentralization. “I propose to view the Web3 community as a decentralization
theater,” he suggests, “namely, a ﬁctitious space whose performers are enjoined to enact decentralization
to preserve the coherence of the play.”[33] Although these modes of “decentralization theatre” are satirical,
they’re memorable enough names that we will adopt them unironically in our analysis:
1. Bucket Decentralization This is a common framing in the blockchain space of decentralization,
whereby it is thought of in economic terms, “equating economic inequality with token ownership
concentration and, by extension, with centralization.” Its logical drawbacks are discussed at length by
Vergne, but for now we simply need to build on to it that in our use we understand it to mean economic
decentralization, particularly that concerned with distribution of voting power (i.e. staked tokens).
2. Godot Decentralization This is another common framing of decentralization, broadly speaking refer-
ring to systemic resilience via technical means, “[f]or some, a system is decentralized when it has so
many points of failure that it simply cannot fail amid adverse circumstances, for any attacker would have
to simultaneously attack on too many fronts to be successful.”
Like in the Gochhayat deﬁnition above, there is a general pattern to responses that to some degree con-
ﬂates systemic robustness or censorship resistance with ‘decentralization’. This is something that we will
return to in our analysis. To begin with, we will adopt a deﬁnition of decentralization that can be summed up
by an interview participant as “there is no one entity that can control the state of information being held by
the blockchain,” while adding to it our hypothesis: “Decentralization, expressed in terms of control of ledger
state, is a holistic expression of the governance layer, that is, on-chain voting power, off-chain coercion, and
social inﬂuence.”
In the spirit of Vergne’s work, our core argument is that actors in the system constitute it and can subvert
it - all the world’s a protocol, and all the men and women merely players.
2.2.1 Bucket Decentralization
Economic decentralization is what Vergne terms ‘Bucket’ decentralization:
“Charlie Bucket, before visiting Willy Wonka’s chocolate factory, lived in extreme poverty. But this kind of
economic inequality would not exist in a truly decentralized system, according to proponents of “Bucket”
deﬁnitions of decentralization...Yet, by equating economic inequality with token ownership concentration
and, by extension, with centralization, “Bucket” deﬁnitions can be quite misleading. First, the wealth of any
given individual is determined by the sum of the value of all the assets they own—not just by the value of
their holdings in one speciﬁc asset (here, cryptocurrency)... A second issue, perhaps even more problem-
atic, is the underlying assumption, made in Bucket conceptualizations, that the dispersion of Lamborghini
ownership is a reasonable proxy to capture the decentralization of the Lamborghini car company.”[33]
We choose to conceptualise this as voting power. Often, number of validator nodes is used as a proxy
for decentralization, as are other metrics like the Nakamoto Coefﬁcient, “the minimum number of entities in a
given subsystem required to get to 51% of the total capacity... [or] the operative threshold”[32], which would
be 66.7% of voting power in Cosmos networks. Both these thresholds were referenced in our ﬁeldwork, both
in the interviews and in free text ﬁelds in the survey. Inequality metrics such as the Gini Coefﬁcient aren’t
more informative than direct analysis of stake distribution for measuring voting power, especially in a situa-
tion where the highest voting power operators tend to accrue more stake, further centralising both stake and
voting power. Cybersecurity researchers like Nick Merrill have observed that the Pareto principle, applies in
the stake and voting power distribution of many of these networks, “[in] the average [Cosmos] DAO, 20% of
the voting weight can (if they so choose) pass a proposal that the remaining 80% of the voting weight op-
poses.”[24]
2.2.2 Godot Decentralization
Vergne’s other relevant deﬁnition is ‘Godot’ decentralization - loosely, what we might call reduction of systemic
risk by technical means. In any case, it eventually reduces down to trust in the technical foundations of the
system, what Gochhayat et al.[14], conceptualise as the network and storage layers:
“For some, a system is decentralized when it has so many points of failure that it simply cannot fail amid
adverse circumstances, for any attacker would have to simultaneously attack on too many fronts to be
3/30

successful. From this perspective, decentralization makes a system resilient in perpetuity— and adver-
saries end up waiting indeﬁnitely for their attacks to reach their objective (like the characters in Beckett’s
Waiting for Godot, who end up waiting indeﬁnitely for the elusive Godot). A limitation of this view is that it
is often trivial to identify a meta-system that encompasses most of the focal system’s agents (or nodes)
and could therefore represent a central point of failure. Take a computer that runs an arbitrary large num-
ber of independent virtual machines; sadly, the hardware that hosts them all represents a single point of
failure. Similarly, a state can decentralize political authority across an arbitrarily large number of elected
representatives; but when they all meet in person to pass laws inside the parliament building, that building
represents a single point of failure (e.g., a bomb could kill them all at once).”[33]
To hardware and network considerations, we add software; both trust in the software itself and of the au-
thors and their organisational processes and resilience. On some of the largest chains such as Ethereum,
large market cap and the availability of multiple protocol implementations, so-called ‘client diversity’, mitigate
some of the risks of centralization at the software layer. This is seen as particularly important for valida-
tor nodes. With multiple implementations, node operators are free to choose between implementations, or
switch in the event of foul play, so the systemic risk posed by a single malicious developer is much smaller.[13]
For ledgers that rely on a global state machine, client diversity is not enough. A ﬁnal important considera-
tion in this discussion is that of smart contracts. Much of the economic activity of the chain occurs at a higher
level than the client, that of smart contracts. Here, development teams are smaller, mistakes are more com-
mon, and exploits more frequent, which can offset the positive software decentralization impacts of client
diversity, for example. Moreover, at runtime, global shared state on the ledger, as has been noted already,
implies a single point of failure.
Our ﬁeldwork also showed common technical metrics were used as heuristics for decentralization by val-
idators. These included geographical distribution of nodes by country, distribution of nodes by data centre
and by vendor, as well as use of different hardware, operating system and internet carrier.
3 RESULTS
What follows are relevant extracts from our survey and semi-structured interviews.
3.1 Semi-structured Interviews - Decentralization
These are responses from our semi-structured interviews to the question, “What do you understand by the
term ‘decentralization’?” They are organised into subsections for ease of referencing.
3.1.1
The idealistic deﬁnition is that there is no central [control], there is no one entity that can control the state
of information being held by the blockchain, so that there’s not a risk of an authoritarian coming in and
rewriting history of some sort. So through decentralization it requires multiple parties to come together
and agree at some threshold to provide consensus on a direction that a chain should go. In a nutshell, it
requires multiple entities to work together to write the chain.
[Prompt: how would you distinguish working together from collusion, if it’s all one type of entity, for
example validators?] There’s typically nothing to stop collusion in that manner. The expectation is that for
somebody to practically collude at that level on a blockchain that has a large number of participants, that
the difﬁculty of the collusion continues to grow as the blockchain grows. However, if the token controlling
interest is held by a select few, sort of like a dev team, and they have a Foundation that is delegating votes,
then in effect they have the controlling interest. I can’t say that this happens or not, but there certainly
could be scenarios in which that’s actually what happens, and there could be collusion, yes.
[Prompt: collusion between the valset against the interests of the Foundation, or between the valida-
tors with delegations and the Foundation?] I would say that whoever has the ability to create the initial set
of tokens and decide on their distribution has the ability to enact some form of collusion, unless it can be
proven that the ownership is in fact distributed and decentralized. Otherwise, it’s highly plausible that the
Foundation could effectively serve as the authoritarian in that instance. Now, collusion amongst individ-
ual validators, there are of course situations where one validator is not actually run by an entity, they are
being run on behalf of another entity, so it looks like they are a unique validator, there could actually be
one group running ten validators with different names, and there’s not really a good way to suss that out
and determine who is actually behind it.
4/30

[Prompt: a Sybil attack?] Yes, exactly.
[Prompt: what is a Foundation in this case?] A Foundation is some sort of steering committee or group
whose members are not directly on the chain, but who can send instructions to the chain, for example, via
治理 tokens that are staked, or via governance tokens that are held. So, if a Foundation has control over the
governance tokens, it can influence the chain. If it doesn’t have control, then the chain is more decentralized.
[Prompts: What’s the difference between a person acting on their own and a person acting via a Foundation?]
They’re acting on their own, but if the Foundation has control over the governance tokens, they can’t be
distinguished from someone acting on their own. So, for example, if a person is acting on their own but
holds a governance token that is staked, then that person can effectively act as a Foundation. So, in that case,
it’s not clear whether that person is acting alone or via the Foundation. That seems to be a key point.
3.1.2
The deﬁnition they have in mind is that a decentralized system has no single point of control, meaning that
there is no one entity that has control over the state of the chain. So, if all the validators are acting in
unison, and the chain state is being written by a consensus mechanism, then the validators are all acting
as a collective, but individually, they don’t have control. So, the system is decentralized because no single
entity has control over the chain state.
But then, the risk is that the validators themselves are controlled by someone else, perhaps a dev team or
a Foundation, so in that case, even though they are acting as a collective, their control is decentralized in
the sense that no single entity is controlling the chain state. But the control of the validators is a separate
issue.
This distinction is important because when the validators are acting in unison, their collective control is a
decentralized control, but if they are controlled by a single entity, that could lead to a situation where that
single entity can manipulate the chain state.
3.1.3
The deﬁnition is that a decentralized system is one where control is distributed, with no single entity
having control over the chain state. So, in the context of a validator, if all validators are acting in unison,
then the state is being written by the collective, but no individual validator has control. So, that’s a good
decentralized system. But if a small number of validators control the majority of the voting power, then
the system is not decentralized because those few validators have control over the chain state.

3.1.4
The ideal deﬁnition is that there is no single point of control. So, the chain is decentralized if no single
node or entity has control over the chain state. But if a single entity owns 51% of the voting power, then
the chain is not decentralized because that entity can control the state. So, the key is whether the chain is
controlled by a single entity or not.

3.2 Decentralization and Governance Topology
3.2.1
The deﬁnition is that a system is decentralized if it has no single point of control, meaning that no single
entity has control over the chain state. So, the validators are acting in unison, but if no single validator has
control, then the system is decentralized. But if a small number of validators control the majority of the
voting power, then the system is not decentralized because those few can control the chain state.
3.3 Semi-structured Interviews - Decentralization
The question is: “What do you understand by the term ‘decentralization’?”
The responses are as follows:
- [A] The system is decentralized if no single entity has control over the chain state.
- [B] Decentralization is when the control is spread out among many entities, so that no single entity has
 control over the chain state.
- [C] Decentralization is when the control is distributed, so that no single entity has control, meaning that
 the system has no single point of failure.
- [D] Decentralization is when there is no single point of control, meaning that the system is controlled by
multiple entities, each with limited control.
- [E] Decentralization is when the control is spread out among many validators, so that no single validator
 has control over the chain state.

return to in our analysis. To begin with, we will adopt a deﬁnition of decentralization that can be summed up
by an interview participant as “there is no one entity that can control the state of information being held by
the blockchain,” while adding to it our hypothesis: “Decentralization, expressed in terms of control of ledger
state, is a holistic expression of the governance layer, that is, on-chain voting power, off-chain coercion, and
social inﬂuence.”
In the spirit of Vergne’s work, our core argument is that actors in the system constitute it and can subvert
it - all the world’s a protocol, and all the men and women merely players.
2.2.1 Bucket Decentralization
Economic decentralization is what Vergne terms ‘Bucket’ decentralization:
“Charlie Bucket, before visiting Willy Wonka’s chocolate factory, lived in extreme poverty. But this kind of
economic inequality would not exist in a truly decentralized system, according to proponents of “Bucket”
deﬁnitions of decentralization...Yet, by equating economic inequality with token ownership concentration
and, by extension, with centralization, “Bucket” deﬁnitions can be quite misleading. First, the wealth of any
given individual is determined by the sum of the value of all the assets they own—not just by the value of
their holdings in one speciﬁc asset (here, cryptocurrency)... A second issue, perhaps even more problem-
atic, is the underlying assumption, made in Bucket conceptualizations, that the dispersion of Lamborghini
ownership is a reasonable proxy to capture the decentralization of the Lamborghini car company.”[33]
We choose to conceptualise this as voting power. Often, number of validator nodes is used as a proxy
for decentralization, as are other metrics like the Nakamoto Coefﬁcient, “the minimum number of entities in a
given subsystem required to get to 51% of the total capacity... [or] the operative threshold”[32], which would
be 66.7% of voting power in Cosmos networks. Both these thresholds were referenced in our ﬁeldwork, both
in the interviews and in free text ﬁelds in the survey. Inequality metrics such as the Gini Coefﬁcient aren’t
more informative than direct analysis of stake distribution for measuring voting power, especially in a situa-
tion where the highest voting power operators tend to accrue more stake, further centralising both stake and
voting power. Cybersecurity researchers like Nick Merrill have observed that the Pareto principle, applies in
the stake and voting power distribution of many of these networks, “[in] the average [Cosmos] DAO, 20% of
the voting weight can (if they so choose) pass a proposal that the remaining 80% of the voting weight op-
poses.”[24]
2.2.2 Godot Decentralization
Vergne’s other relevant deﬁnition is ‘Godot’ decentralization - loosely, what we might call reduction of systemic
risk by technical means. In any case, it eventually reduces down to trust in the technical foundations of the
system, what Gochhayat et al.[14], conceptualise as the network and storage layers:
“For some, a system is decentralized when it has so many points of failure that it simply cannot fail amid
adverse circumstances, for any attacker would have to simultaneously attack on too many fronts to be
3/30

successful. From this perspective, decentralization makes a system resilient in perpetuity— and adver-
saries end up waiting indeﬁnitely for their attacks to reach their objective (like the characters in Beckett’s
Waiting for Godot, who end up waiting indeﬁnitely for the elusive Godot). A limitation of this view is that it
is often trivial to identify a meta-system that encompasses most of the focal system’s agents (or nodes)
and could therefore represent a central point of failure. Take a computer that runs an arbitrary large num-
ber of independent virtual machines; sadly, the hardware that hosts them all represents a single point of
failure. Similarly, a state can decentralize political authority across an arbitrarily large number of elected
representatives; but when they all meet in person to pass laws inside the parliament building, that building
represents a single point of failure (e.g., a bomb could kill them all at once).”[33]
To hardware and network considerations, we add software; both trust in the software itself and of the au-
thors and their organisational processes and resilience. On some of the largest chains such as Ethereum,
large market cap and the availability of multiple protocol implementations, so-called ‘client diversity’, mitigate
some of the risks of centralization at the software layer. This is seen as particularly important for valida-
tor nodes. With multiple implementations, node operators are free to choose between implementations, or
switch in the event of foul play, so the systemic risk posed by a single malicious developer is much smaller.[13]
For ledgers that rely on a global state machine, client diversity is not enough. A ﬁnal important considera-
tion in this discussion is that of smart contracts. Much of the economic activity of the chain occurs at a higher
level than the client, that of smart contracts. Here, development teams are smaller, mistakes are more com-
mon, and exploits more frequent, which can offset the positive software decentralization impacts of client
diversity, for example. Moreover, at runtime, global shared state on the ledger, as has been noted already,
implies a single point of failure.
Our ﬁeldwork also showed common technical metrics were used as heuristics for decentralization by val-
idators. These included geographical distribution of nodes by country, distribution of nodes by data centre
and by vendor, as well as use of different hardware, operating system and internet carrier.

In the multiple-choice survey, a free-text ﬁeld was provided for respondents to supply their own deﬁnition of

facetious, “I do not understand anything”, while some were very speciﬁc, “Everything not being controlled by

4 ANALYSIS
4.1 Agents in the System
An analysis of typical agents in the system is necessary to understand the governance topology described
in these interviews. Given that decentralization is at least partly a description of agents in the system and
their incentives, these entities and their incentives require enumeration. This list of stakeholders for a typical
Proof-of-Stake network is deﬁned below.
4.1.1 Agents
We deﬁne ﬁve personas, Foundation, Developers, Contributors, Validators and Stakers. As we focus on
Proof-of-Stake systems, we omit users, as stakers are a subset of users who directly interact with the in-
centive mechanisms of economic ﬁnality and chain governance via staking.
These personas interact in complex and unpredictable ways.
1. Foundation
Catch-all term for a central control entity.
For Venture Capital or institution-backed blockchain projects, there is often an entity set up to execute
core business, development, and hold tokens, manage payroll et cetera. Since a foundation in the Cay-
mans is commonly used for this, the colloquialism Foundation has come to be used for any formal entity
nominally in charge of stewarding a blockchain project; “these foundations are...created in Switzerland
or other crypto-friendly countries.”[23] “The standard theory of crypto foundations is that they are like
governments with respect to a national or regional economy, i.e. raising a public treasury and allocat-
ing resources to blockchain speciﬁc capital works, education, R&D, etc., to beneﬁt the community and
develop the ecosystem.”[29]
A more blunt deﬁnition can be found in our transcripts, “[y]ou’re trying to distinguish between two
organisations. The development team and the Foundation. A blockchain Foundation is what I believe
is a quasi-comical legal attempt to separate diverse executives and the lion’s share of economic value
in the form of tokens and ﬁat currency from the actual programmatic operations of the blockchain itself.
So blockchains as a whole, they have management, executives and non-technological operations, and
then they also have operations, and technical development operations and devops. They will attempt to
split those two buckets apart, the non-technology from the technology, in some way to try to be at arm’s
length in case regulators or the government comes after them. They can say that ‘oh we’re not really
doing this, it’s these other people,’ y’know, ‘go shoot the developers,’ right?” (Interview participant)
2. Core Team
The wider control entity and operations team, which in many cases will include the developers of the
software.
Where there is no formal Foundation, core team refers to the same stewardship group. This can depend
on the stage of the project, “at the early stage of a project, that project [may not] even have a Founda-
tion yet. Foundations [are] typically established at the beginning of the mainnet launch. That’s when
the project is getting serious, then they want a separate two entities. The Foundation is [say] a Swiss
entity, and the core team can be a US team.” (Interview participant) Sometimes, in the situation where a
Foundation has a more complex structure there might be a distinction between a Foundation that holds
tokens at genesis and a company or core team that work on the roadmap for the blockchain. The code-
base will almost certainly be open source software, since node operators are expected to check the
integrity of software before it is run (see Figure 2).
In the Cosmos Ecosystem, every major chain is open source, as can be seen from the repository
sections: references in the chain registry directory[15].
